before.exam_tip_html: For a ‘4 marks — Describe Two Features’ question on post-war austerity, give two distinct features with specific supporting detail for each. For example: “One feature was food rationing, which continued until 1954 and included restrictions on meat, butter, and sugar. A second feature was the housing shortage, with an estimated three million homes needing repair and families waiting years for council housing.” Avoid vague answers such as “life was hard” — examiners reward precise factual knowledge. For 8-mark significance questions, address both significance at the time and significance over time: the welfare state mattered immediately for ordinary people’s health and security, and its long-term significance lies in establishing principles of universal entitlement that shaped British politics for decades.

On questions asking you to explain a cause or consequence, be specific about the time period — the examiner wants to see you distinguish between medieval, early modern and modern explanations. Don’t just say ‘people believed in miasma’: say when, give an example of how it shaped behaviour (such as the beaked masks in 1665), and explain why this view persisted. For 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ questions, you must show the change over time and link it to a factor such as science, technology or government action.

When answering questions about why the Crusades happened, examiners want you to connect the power of the papacy to the call for crusade. Don’t just describe Cluniac reform in isolation — explain how it strengthened papal authority, which then made Urban II’s appeal possible. For 8-mark significance questions, remember to address significance at the time (e.g. Canossa immediately weakened Henry IV) and over time (e.g. papal supremacy shaped European politics for centuries).

For questions on the causes of the First Crusade, you must connect the political context (Seljuk expansion, Byzantine appeal) with the ideological context (Cluniac reform, holy war, pilgrimage) and Urban II’s specific actions at Clermont. Examiners want you to weigh these factors — don’t just list them. For the 10-mark “Why do interpretations differ?” question type, be ready to explain why historians debate whether religious faith or material motives were more important for crusaders.

Questions about the explorers often test the 8-mark “Explain Change” type: here you must explain what changed as a result of these voyages, not just describe what happened. Think about what changed for European trade routes (Lisbon replaced Venice), for geographical knowledge (confirmation that America was a separate continent; the Earth’s circumference confirmed by Magellan), and for indigenous populations. For 6-mark cause/consequence questions, always link your evidence directly to the specific cause or consequence you are explaining — examiners reward explicit causal links, not just description.

The 16-mark thematic change essay is likely to ask how far the nature of crime changed across all three eras. To reach the top band, cover the medieval era (petty theft, violence), the early modern era (vagrancy, heresy, collective protest), and the modern era (car crime, terrorism, cybercrime). A common mistake is treating the nineteenth century as ‘modern’ — examiners want you to reach the twentieth or twenty-first century for full credit. Show continuity too: poverty-driven crime and property crime persist in every era even as new categories emerge.

For questions about law enforcement before 1829, examiners want you to understand why the system was so weak — not just describe it. The key points are: it was unpaid, part-time and community-based; it worked in small rural communities but broke down in larger towns; it depended on property-owners enforcing laws that protected their own interests. For the 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ question comparing medieval to early modern enforcement, focus on the shift from pure community responsibility (tithing, hue and cry) to a more formalised but still amateur system (constable, JP).

For questions about the Final Solution, handle with precision: name the Wannsee Conference (January 1942), the Einsatzgruppen killings in the Soviet Union from 1941, and the death camps in occupied Poland. Avoid vague references — examiners reward specific evidence. For significance questions on the July Plot or White Rose, remember to assess both contemporary significance (immediate impact on the regime) and long-term significance (how they are remembered and what they reveal about the limits of dissent).

For questions about advances in medical knowledge, you need to be clear about what was new and what it replaced. When writing about Vesalius or Harvey, explain what was wrong before (Galenic theory) and why the new knowledge was significant. For DNA and germ theory, link to broader consequences: germ theory enabled vaccines and antiseptics; DNA knowledge is enabling targeted therapies. Examiners reward responses that track the knock-on consequences of new knowledge, not just descriptions of the discovery itself.

For ‘Explain Significance’ questions on a battle like the Somme, always cover significance at the time (the immediate casualties and shock at home) AND over time (what tactical lessons were learned; how the battle contributed to Allied victory in 1918). For ‘Compare Two Sources’ questions on the Western Front, focus on what each source tells you, who produced it and why — not just which one you ‘agree with’. Examiners want you to weigh utility for a specific historical enquiry.

For the 8-mark ‘Explain Change’ question on twentieth-century policing, focus on a specific technology (fingerprinting from 1901, DNA profiling from 1984) or a specific development (999 system 1937, specialist units, community policing). Examiners want you to explain how the change improved policing, not just name it. For a 16-mark thematic essay comparing policing across all eras, the shift from community responsibility (Saxon tithings) to professional forces (1829) to technological/specialised policing (twentieth century) is the key three-era framework — make sure you argue a judgement about which change was most significant.

When answering questions on the military orders or castle technology, link your knowledge back to the wider crusading story. Why did military orders emerge? Because of the manpower problem. Why did castle design improve? Because of the experience of sieges in the First Crusade and the need to defend long frontiers with small armies. Examiners reward explanations that connect details to the broader context rather than isolated description. For 8-mark significance questions, remember to address both contemporary and long-term significance.

When assessing whether the 1920s truly changed the role of women, examiners want you to weigh the genuine changes (the vote, the flapper, birth control access, more women in the workforce) against the significant limits (the Nineteenth Amendment excluded Black women in practice; flappers were a minority; wages still lower than men; conservative backlash). For 8-mark significance questions about the Nineteenth Amendment or the flapper, always address both the significance at the time and the limits — this is where top-band responses are won. For a 12-mark ‘How far do you agree’ question, the flapper as evidence of change but the continued exclusion of working-class and Black women as evidence of limits are your strongest analytical tools.

For questions on punishment, examiners want you to explain the purpose behind each method, not just describe it. Deterrence, retribution and public shaming are the key concepts for the medieval and early modern periods. For the 16-mark thematic essay, the shift from public/physical punishment (mutilation, stocks, public execution) to imprisonment and rehabilitation (nineteenth century onwards) is the central change — make sure you can explain why attitudes changed, not just that they did.

When answering questions about modern public health, show awareness of the shift in the nature of health problems across the twentieth century: from infectious diseases (tuberculosis, cholera) to non-communicable lifestyle diseases (heart disease, cancer, obesity). Examiners reward responses that show this transition rather than treating all health threats as the same type. For thematic essays, link modern campaigns (smoking ban, Change4Life) back to the same underlying driver as Victorian sanitation — government responding to evidence that preventable conditions are killing people — to show change and continuity together.

For questions on prison reform, name specific reformers (John Howard, Elizabeth Fry), specific dates (Howard’s 1777 publication; Pentonville 1842) and specific innovations (separate system, silent system). Examiners want you to evaluate as well as describe: was the separate system successful? (No — it caused mental breakdowns.) Was Elizabeth Fry’s approach different from Howard’s? (Yes — she added rehabilitation to Howard’s humanitarian improvements.) For the 16-mark thematic essay on punishment, the shift from public/physical punishment to imprisonment is the key nineteenth-century change.

This synthesis lesson is your preparation for the 16-mark thematic change essay. The most common error is treating the essay as a chronological list of changes rather than a structured argument. The examiner wants you to identify the most important factor (or turning point) and argue for it with evidence across all three eras. A strong answer will: name a factor (e.g. technology), explain how it drove change in the medieval, early modern and modern eras with specific examples, weigh it against continuity and against other factors, and reach a substantiated overall conclusion. No factor is the “right” answer — what matters is the quality of argument and evidence.

For the 16-mark thematic change essay, the examiner is looking for two things above all else: coverage of all three eras (medieval, early modern, modern) AND a structured argument about the balance of change and continuity. Don’t just list events in order — organise your answer around one or two key factors (e.g. ‘science was the biggest driver of change, but government action was needed to make discoveries reach the whole population’) and use evidence from all three eras to support your argument. A conclusion that weighs change against continuity and reaches a substantiated judgement is essential for the top band.

For 16-mark period essays, use the PEEL paragraph structure for each factor (Point, Evidence, Explain the link to the question, Link to overall argument). But the most important ingredient is a substantiated overall judgement — clearly argued, at the end, after you have weighed both sides. Examiners reward a specific, reasoned conclusion more than a list of balanced points without a decision. Use language like: 'Of these changes, the most significant was... because... whereas the other changes, though important, were...'
